issues.legal_issue: The restriction on taking cognizance of document-related offences applies only when the offence was committed after the document was produced or given in evidence in court.
material_facts: The alleged will was said to have been forged before it was filed in probate proceedings.
The complainants initiated a private criminal complaint alleging forgery and related offences.
There was no allegation that an offence concerning the will was committed after it had been filed in court.
issues.conclusion: The restriction did not prevent cognizance on the private complaint because the alleged forgery preceded the will’s production in court. The court’s complaint is required only when the specified document-related offence is committed after the document has been produced or given in evidence.
issues.legal_principle: Section 195(1)(b)(ii) CrPC requires a complaint by the court for the specified document-related offences only when they are committed after the document has been produced or given in evidence in court. Section 190 provides the general routes to cognizance, while Sections 340–343 prescribe the court-complaint procedure. The Court approved Sachida Nand Singh v. State of Bihar and explained that Surjit Singh v. Balbir Singh did not lay down a contrary rule; it also relied on Patel Lalji Bhai Somabhai v. State of Gujarat, Raghunath v. State of U.P., and related earlier decisions concerning the corresponding provision in the former Code.

predicates.document_offence_prosecution: A criminal proceeding concerns an alleged offence involving a document produced or given in evidence in a court proceeding.
predicates.document_offence_after_production: The alleged document-related offence was committed after the document had been produced or given in evidence in court.

issues.definition: When a document-offence prosecution concerns an offence committed after the document was produced or given in evidence, a court complaint is required for cognizance.

issues.legal_issue: Findings in civil proceedings do not bind criminal proceedings merely because both concern the same alleged conduct.
material_facts: The alleged forgery was disputed in probate proceedings and was also the subject of a criminal complaint.
The civil and criminal proceedings would apply different standards of proof and decide their cases on the evidence presented in each.
issues.conclusion: There is no statutory provision or legal principle making findings in one proceeding final or binding in the other; the possibility of conflicting findings is not, by itself, a reason to prevent the criminal proceeding.
issues.legal_principle: Civil cases are decided on the preponderance of evidence, while criminal cases require proof beyond reasonable doubt, with the burden on the prosecution. The Court relied on M.S. Sheriff v. State of Madras for the principle that the possibility of conflicting decisions is not itself a relevant reason to defer one proceeding, and that the proceedings are decided independently on their evidence.

predicates.civil_and_criminal_proceedings: Civil and criminal proceedings address the same or related alleged conduct.
predicates.each_proceeding_has_its_own_evidence: Each proceeding is decided on the evidence adduced in that proceeding.

issues.definition: When related civil and criminal proceedings are each decided on their own evidence, a finding in one does not bind the other.

issues.legal_issue: A court is not required to make a criminal complaint in every case involving an offence affecting the administration of justice; it must consider whether a complaint is expedient in the interests of justice.
material_facts: An application had been made asking the probate court to file a criminal complaint concerning the allegedly forged will.
The judgment explained that the effect of the alleged offence on the administration of justice, rather than only the magnitude of injury to the affected person, guides the court’s assessment.
issues.conclusion: A court complaint is discretionary and should be made when the court considers an inquiry expedient in the interests of justice, having regard to the offence’s effect on the administration of justice.
issues.legal_principle: Section 340(1) CrPC conditions the court’s power to complain on its opinion that an inquiry is expedient in the interests of justice. The Court explained that this assessment normally concerns the effect or impact of the alleged offence on the administration of justice, not merely the magnitude of injury suffered by the affected person.

predicates.court_considers_a_complaint_about_an_adm: A court is asked to initiate a complaint about an alleged offence affecting the administration of justice.
predicates.justice_expediency_is_assessed: The court considers whether an inquiry is expedient in the interests of justice, including the alleged offence’s impact on the administration of justice.

issues.definition: When a court considers such a complaint and assesses whether an inquiry is expedient in the interests of justice, filing the complaint is not automatic.

issues.legal_issue: The rule of strict construction applicable to penal statutes does not govern a procedural provision that restricts cognizance of specified offences.
material_facts: The disputed provision limits when a criminal court may take cognizance without a complaint from a court.
The provision is part of criminal procedure and does not itself create an offence or impose a penalty.
issues.conclusion: The provision is procedural rather than penal, so the asserted rule of strict construction for penal statutes does not apply to its interpretation.
issues.legal_principle: The Court distinguished a procedural bar on cognizance from a penal statute creating an offence or imposing a penalty. It relied on Lalita Jalan v. Bombay Gas Co. and the decisions discussed there, including Murlidhar Meghraj Loya v. State of Maharashtra, Kisan Trimbak Kothula v. State of Maharashtra, Superintendent and Remembrancer of Legal Affairs v. Abani Maity, and State of Maharashtra v. Natwarlal Damodardas Soni, in explaining that statutory construction should suppress the mischief and advance the legislative object.

predicates.cognizance_restriction_is_procedural: The provision restricts the procedure for taking cognizance but does not create an offence or impose a penalty.

issues.definition: When a cognizance restriction is procedural rather than penal, strict penal construction does not apply.
